title: Freya and the House
premise: Ansel Fairweather, a pest controller who inherited their grandmother's house and its inexplicable noises, has spent seven years rationalizing every anomaly—until the photographs begin showing an extra chair that no one remembers buying. The chair belongs to the House itself, an entity that has been patiently composing a family out of borrowed memories, and it has decided Ansel is the final member. To escape, Ansel must learn the lullaby the House hums through the floorboards, find its missing last verse hidden in grandma's effects, and sing it back without joining in—because the House only keeps those who harmonize. In the end, Ansel completes the verse alone in the cellar, refuses to sing along when the House offers them everything they've ever lacked, and walks out as the walls collapse into silence; the last chapter reveals the House has simply begun again, humming, in a new house down the road.
about_author: Xanthe Crane is the pen name of a former building surveyor who spent a decade cataloguing structural defects in Victorian houses and swears three of them were not defects. They write horror about architecture that notices its occupants.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. A routine pest-control job at a neighbor's house ends with Ansel hearing the same three-note hum they hear at home. They tell themselves it's water pipes. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter in Ansel's POV: inheriting grandma's house, the first scratching in the walls, the list of rationalizations taped inside a kitchen cabinet. Establishes Ansel's coping strategy of staying small and invisible. Beat: fragile control.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Sorting grandma's photo albums, Ansel finds every picture now contains a wooden chair that wasn't there before—older photos, newer photos, all of them. POV Ansel. Beat: reality's seams splitting open.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Ansel dusts the house for prints and finds small handprints on the ceiling, at child height, leading nowhere. Their professional tools confirm what their mind denies. Beat: the rationalist toolkit fails.

chapters.title: The Song Through the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Nighttime. The house hums a lullaby Ansel half-remembers from childhood, and catches themselves humming along before stopping cold. POV Ansel. Beat: complicity discovered—the horror is participatory.

chapters.title: Neighborly Advice
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Marisol Vega, the neighbor from chapter one, who admits her family left their own humming house decades ago and warns Ansel: 'It doesn't haunt you. It adopts you.' Beat: Ansel learns this is a pattern, not a haunting.

chapters.title: Grandma's Locked Drawer
chapters.summary: Ansel finally opens the drawer grandma always kept locked: sheet music titled 'Fairweather Lullaby,' two verses written, the third torn out. Beat: hope—a possible exit exists.

chapters.title: What the House Offers
chapters.summary: The house begins granting small mercies: a broken boiler fixed overnight, grief dreams replaced by warm ones, a memory of grandma's voice that may be real or planted. POV Ansel. Beat: temptation; belonging weaponized.

chapters.title: Marisol's Photographs
chapters.summary: Marisol shares her family's old albums: same extra chair, same slow addition of figures. Her aunt appears in photos taken after she vanished. Beat: stakes clarified—the House keeps people permanently.

chapters.title: The Verse in the Walls
chapters.summary: Following the hum, Ansel pries open a wall cavity and finds a child's notebook—grandma's, aged nine—with the third verse copied in pencil, but the page is blank where the words should be. Beat: cruel near-miss.

chapters.title: Invisible No Longer
chapters.summary: The house stops pretending. Doors rearrange, rooms repeat, and the chair sits at the head of the table set for dinner. The House speaks for the first time—not in words, but by replaying Ansel's loneliest memories as invitations. Beat: power revealed; corruption of comfort.

chapters.title: The Previous Tenants
chapters.summary: Research chapter, dual POV via letters found in the attic: 1940s tenants describe the same song, the same offer, and one who 'stayed happily.' Ansel realizes some residents chose this. Beat: horror of consent.

chapters.title: Marisol Disappears
chapters.summary: Marisol stops answering; her porch light burns; through the window Ansel sees her sitting in an identical chair, smiling, eyes wrong. Beat: loss and terror—the pattern completing itself.

chapters.title: The Cellar Door Opens
chapters.summary: A door that was always painted shut now stands open. Descending, Ansel finds the house's root: a room where every stolen memory hangs like laundry, including ones Ansel thought were their own. Beat: identity crisis—who curated Ansel's life?

chapters.title: Half-Sung
chapters.summary: Desperate, Ansel attempts the lullaby with the two known verses. The house leans in, delighted—and begins singing harmony, trying to pull Ansel into the third verse's rhythm without the words. Ansel barely stops. Beat: climax rehearsal; the danger of singing along made visceral.

chapters.title: Asking Grandma
chapters.summary: Using the memory-room, Ansel reconstructs grandma's final year and learns she tore out the verse deliberately: the last lines are a choice, sung differently by each person, which is why they can't be found—only composed. Beat: revelation; agency restored.

chapters.title: The House Bargains
chapters.summary: The House makes its full offer: grandma alive in memory, loneliness ended, a family completed—everything, forever, if Ansel just finishes the song together. POV Ansel, wavering genuinely. Beat: dark night of the soul.

chapters.title: Composing the Last Verse
chapters.summary: Alone at dawn, Ansel writes the third verse from their own life—the true one, unedited by the House—including the parts that hurt. Beat: reclaiming identity; the theme of belonging answered on Ansel's terms.

chapters.title: The Singing
chapters.summary: Climax. In the cellar, Ansel sings all three verses while the House throws every temptation into the melody. Ansel sings the last verse to the House rather than with it—an act of witness, not surrender. The walls scream, then listen. Beat: peak tension.

chapters.title: Silence
chapters.summary: The house lets go. Rooms return to their true shapes; the chair is gone from every photograph; Marisol wakes on her porch, hollowed but alive. Ansel packs, leaves the keys, and does not look back. Beat: release and grief entwined.

chapters.title: What Belonging Costs
chapters.summary: Epilogue-adjacent. Ansel, renting a plain apartment that hums with nothing, visits Marisol and begins telling the truth about what happened. Beat: quiet resolution; belonging rebuilt human-sized.

chapters.title: Humming Down the Road
chapters.summary: Final chapter, omniscient POV. Three streets over, a new family unpacks in a Victorian house. At midnight, the floorboards begin, softly, to hum. Beat: cyclical dread; the corruption of power persists.
